3.text: wooden barracks and a high tower, standing apart, on the cape. Both are

4.text: still standing at the present time. The tower is called by the people “Laptev’s

5.text: Beacon).” They say that a fire was burning on the top of this tower as a

6.text: beacon for Laptev’s people straggling in the desert, though the top of Thick

7.text: Cape is much higher than the top of the tower, and more open to view, so

8.text: that there was no need of a special wooden tower.

9.text: I will also mention two merchants of Yakutsk, Shalaurov and Bakhov,

10.text: who in 1755-64 went on several expeditions from the mouth of the Lena

11.text: River eastwards. They went for trading-purposes, and got as far as Cape

12.text: Erri. There they perished, with all their companions. The so-called Shalaurov

13.text: barracks, which they built for use during one of those winters, are also still

14.text: standing on the Lower Kolyma shore, near the ocean.

15.text: Cessation of War. — The expedition of Pavlutsky was the last military

16.text: enterprise of the Russians against the Chukchee. Shortly after that the

17.text: Government decided to abandon a plan which turned out to be so difficult

18.text: and expensive, and which did not promise any valuable results.

19.text: Mr. Jochelson’s surmise that the cessation of Russian expeditions to the

20.text: country of the Chukchee was due to the fact that the latter were poor in

21.text: objects of tribute,¹ may be corroborated by evidence.

22.text: Thus numerous reports of the Cossacks and public-service men, some of

23.text: which I have already quoted, repeat always, “There [in the country of the

24.text: Chukchee] is no game except wolves and red foxes, and even these are scarce

25.text: because of the lack of wood.” In answer to these reports, the Government

26.text: issued orders as follows: “You are to go there to the unpeaceful Chukchee,

27.text: and request them to bow down under the Czar’s high hand, to the eternal

28.text: payment of tribute, and to take from them an oath of allegiance to arrange

29.text: register-books and to have them taxed with tribute according to those books;

30.text: and if in that country sables and foxes are really scarce, take for tribute

32.text: Seventeen years after the death of Pavlutsky began the breaking-up of

33.text: the Russian military reign in the extreme northeast of Siberia. The fortress

34.text: of Anadyrsk was given up in the year 1764. The Governor-General of East

35.text: Siberia says in his report of Nov. 24, 1792, “The fortress of Anadyrsk, which

36.text: existed during the years 1710-64, cost the Treasury 539,246 rubles, and it

37.text: also caused a loss of 841,760 rubles to various peoples who had to carry

38.text: Government freight, the total expenses being 1,381,607 rubles; revenue for

39.text: the whole time, 29,152 rubles. For this reason it was abandoned in 1764.”³

42.text: soon exhausted. The Reindeer Chukchee, who were the nearest to the Russian forts, and against whom the

43.text: war was chiefly directed, did not even have walrus-tusks.
